text: You've filtered rows, projected columns, and aggregated with summarize. This last lesson of the chapter adds two more pieces: a real time window with ago, and join, which combines two separate tables into one correlated result — the two ingredients almost every real Sentinel hunting query is actually built from.

ago(24h) returns the timestamp 24 hours before the moment the query runs, so this keeps only sign-ins from the last day. You've already used ago(1d) and ago(7d) in earlier lessons — filtering on TimeGenerated right at the top of a query keeps Log Analytics from scanning far more data than you actually need.

join combines rows from two tables based on a matching column, the same idea as a SQL join. kind=inner keeps only rows with a match on both sides — here, only sign-ins whose IPAddress also appears as a NetworkIP in Sentinel's threat intelligence feed. Notice the right-hand table gets its own ago(24h) filter before the join even happens, which is what keeps a join like this fast against tables with millions of rows.

Add project and this becomes a real, usable hunting query. Every row in the result is a sign-in in the last 24 hours from an IP address threat intelligence already flagged, paired with ThreatType and Description explaining exactly why — filter, join, and project combined into one correlation.

Inside the on clause, dollar-left refers to the table before join, SigninLogs here, and dollar-right refers to the table inside the parentheses, ThreatIntelligenceIndicator. You need that prefix whenever the two tables' join columns have different names, exactly like IPAddress and NetworkIP in this query.

That's the whole chapter's toolkit — where, project, summarize, and now join — in one query. Chapter 3 picks up right here: Lesson 9 takes a KQL query like this one and turns it into a scheduled analytics rule, so Sentinel runs it automatically and raises an incident on its own.
